title: Automating meeting notes without losing the relationship
metaTitle: Meeting notes a client can still correct
excerpt: Turn a client call into decisions, open questions, owners, and dates. A person who was there checks the note before the client sees it.
alt: A cream sofa between two bright windows, with a framed abstract painting and teal vases. Meeting notes should leave the room this calm: decisions, owners, and nothing invented.
caption: A calm room for a record of what was actually decided. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Should meeting notes be a transcript?
faqs.answer: The note a client sees should be decisions, open questions, owners, and dates. A transcript is evidence for the reviewer, not the deliverable. If a decision was fuzzy on the call, the note should stay fuzzy.

faqs.question: Who has to read the notes before the client does?
faqs.answer: A person who was on the call. Someone who was not there can check grammar and cannot check the agreement. Prices, dates, and scope lines need that read every time, because a sharper sentence can become an accidental contract.

faqs.question: What if the client says the note is wrong?
faqs.answer: Change the note. Their correction wins over a polished summary, even if you keep the recording for your own check. Do not paste a transcript into the thread to win the point. Say that you updated the record, and keep one home for the current version.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Meeting notes automation should turn a client call into a short record of decisions, open questions, owners, and dates. A person who was on the call reads that record before the client does. The transcript can be long. The note the client sees has to be something they can correct in one reply.

Automate the handoff around the notes, not the relationship that happened on the call. The machine may record, with consent, and draft the four-part note from what was actually said. Keep a person on anything the client will see, anything that states a price or a promise, and anything you would struggle to undo once they start working from it. Then compare the minutes you used to spend writing the note with the minutes you spend fixing a wrong one.

## What the note is for

The note is a memory both sides can use next week. It is not a performance of how thorough the studio is, and it is not a transcript with the filler removed by a model that wants to sound organized. If a decision was fuzzy on the call, the note says it was fuzzy. Cleaning it into a firm decision is how scope changes without anyone noticing.

Agree the shape before you pick a tool. Four headings are enough.

- Decisions: what you agreed, in sentences a stranger could follow.
- Open questions: what you did not agree, with who will answer.
- Owners: names, not "the team."
- Dates: only dates someone said, including "no date yet."

Anything else, including a theme, a mood, or a paragraph of advice the model thought you meant, stays out. If you need a longer debrief inside the studio, that is a different document and the client does not receive it by default.

Hanabi keeps client files, decisions, and updates in a portal after delivery so the record has a home that is not a private inbox. The note can land there once a person has checked it. Landing there before the check means the client may treat a draft as the agreement.

## Consent, capture, and the draft

Say, at the start of the call, that you will record or transcribe so the notes are accurate, and say who will see them. A person says it. A tool that joins the call in silence and emails a summary to the client is a surprise, and surprises are a poor way to keep a relationship. If the client declines, you take notes by hand and the automation does not get a recording to invent from.

The draft may quote short phrases. It may not upgrade a hedge. "We could look at a second page" is not "We will add a second page." "Probably next month" is not a launch date. Write the instruction to the tool in those terms, and keep an example of a hedge that must survive. People speak in hedges because the decision is not made. The note's job is to preserve that.

Name the source of each important line in a way the reviewer can check. A timestamp, or a short quote, is enough. A reviewer who cannot find the moment in the recording will either trust the model or rewrite the note from scratch. One of those is dangerous. The other means you saved no time.

Store the recording where the studio can delete it on the schedule you told the client. An archive you forgot about is not a feature. The note is the thing you meant to keep. The recording is the evidence for the review, and then it can go.

## What a person checks before anyone else sees it

The client will see this note. A person who was on the call is the only one who can tell whether a sentence is true. Someone who was not in the room can check grammar. They cannot check the agreement.

The review is a pass over four risks.

1. A decision appears that nobody made. Delete it, or move it to open questions.
2. A price, a date, or a scope line is sharper than the conversation. Restore the hedge, or write "not agreed."
3. An owner is wrong, or a client-side owner was volunteered without them accepting it.
4. The next step is something you cannot undo, such as starting a build, sending an invoice, or emailing a third party. Those wait for a direct confirmation, not for a summary.

Send the note from the person who was on the call. A sender named "notes bot" tells the client the record was unattended. Invite a correction in one line: if a decision is wrong, reply and the note will change. Then mean it. The correction wins over the recording when the client says the words were theirs and the meaning was not. You can keep the recording for your own check. You do not argue with their correction by pasting a transcript into the thread.

Nielsen Norman Group's article [How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is a useful limit on length. People often leave a page in 10 to 20 seconds, a visit averages a little less than a minute, and readers get through only about a quarter of the text. A client will not read a twelve-section recap. They will read decisions and dates if those are first. Put them first. The open questions come next. A narrative of the call comes last, or not at all.

## Prices, scope, and other lines you do not automate

A note that says you agreed a price is a commercial document, even when you meant it as minutes. Keep that line on a person's read every time, including after the workflow has been quiet for months. The same goes for a promise to hit a date, a promise to include a feature, and a promise to introduce them to someone else.

Do not let the tool file the note into a task system as assignments for the client. Creating work on their side is hard to undo, and it often misreads a suggestion as a request. Your internal tasks can be drafted. Their tasks wait until they have seen the note and accepted them.

Do not let the tool email the note to a wider list than the people on the call. Adding a founder, an investor, or another vendor "for context" is a disclosure. A person chooses that list. The default is the people who spoke.

Do not ask the model to produce action items "so the meeting feels productive" when the meeting was a review with no new decisions. An empty decision list is a successful note. Filling it is how a calm call becomes a fake plan.

If you want a second person to pressure-test the way your studio handles this kind of boundary, book an [intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring one recent call and the note you wish you had sent. The decision on that call is whether a drafted record would have helped or would have needed a rewrite.

## Minutes saved against minutes of repair

Time five notes written the old way, including the delay between the call and the writing. Delay matters. Notes written the next afternoon already contain guesses. The automation's gift, when it works, is a draft ready while the call is still fresh, not a prettier prose style.

Time the repair. How long to listen back, delete invented decisions, and send? If repair takes longer than writing a short note yourself, change the output. Ask for the four headings only, with quotes, and stop asking for a narrative. Many teams save time only after they forbid the summary paragraph.

Count corrections from clients for a month. A correction is not a failure by itself. A client who fixes a name is healthy. A client who writes "we did not agree to that" is a failed draft. If you see more than a rare one of those, stop sending notes until the instruction to the tool is stricter. The relationship cost of a false agreement is larger than the cost of slow notes.

Keep the recording review on the first twenty calls even if you are proud of the drafts. Confident inventions are the failure mode: a date that was an example, a feature that was a question, a compliment rewritten as a requirement. After twenty clean notes, a lighter pass is reasonable on internal-only drafts. Client-facing notes still get the four-risk check.

## Where the note lives after you send it

Put the checked note where you will both look next time. A portal page, a shared document, or the top of the project thread. One home. A note that also lives in email, in a bot, and in a slide will drift, and the drift will be blamed on the person who was careful.

When the note changes because the client corrected it, change the home, and say that you changed it. Do not leave the old version attached to the original email as if both are true. If a later call reverses a decision, the new note says what replaced it. The automation can draft that update from the new call. It cannot decide that the old decision "still basically stands."

Retire the workflow for a client who asks you not to record. Take the notes yourself. Offer the same four headings so the record stays familiar. The point was never the recording. The point was a memory you can both use without a fight about what was said.

The next handoff is the draft that is waiting on the client, not the notes of the call that produced it. [Automating content approval without losing the relationship](/blog/automating-content-approval-without-losing-the-relationship) follows, because a reminder about a document can nag, publish, or misread a comment if you let the timer make the decision.
